decks.domain: Traffic laws: speed, signaling, lanes, turns, roundabouts, J-turns, U-turns and passing

cards.front: Who do Minnesota's traffic laws apply to?
cards.back: Minnesota's traffic laws cover every person who drives on a public road anywhere in the state.

cards.front: When may you leave the right side of a wide road?
cards.back: On roads of sufficient width you keep to the right side unless you are passing a vehicle going your way, the right side is closed for construction or repair, the road has three marked lanes, signs make it one-way, or you are moving over for a stopped authorized vehicle under the Move Over Law.

cards.front: What does the basic speed law require?
cards.back: Under the basic speed law your speed must be reasonable for the current weather, traffic and road conditions, and the posted limit is the highest speed allowed on that road.

cards.front: Is it legal to drive below a posted minimum speed in normal conditions?
cards.back: Where a minimum speed limit is posted, driving below it under normal conditions is illegal.

cards.front: What is the default speed limit in an alley?
cards.back: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit in an alley under ideal conditions is ten miles per hour

cards.front: What is the default speed limit on urban or town roads?
cards.back: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit on urban or town roads under ideal conditions is thirty miles per hour

cards.front: What is the default speed limit where no other default applies?
cards.back: Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit under ideal conditions is fifty-five miles per hour in every location not otherwise listed.

cards.front: What must you do in school zones and work zones?
cards.back: In a school zone you must slow down when children are present, and in a work or construction zone you must slow down and drive carefully.

cards.front: What are the three default speed limits under ideal conditions?
cards.back: The three default limits under ideal conditions are ten miles per hour in alleys, thirty miles per hour on urban or town roads and fifty-five miles per hour everywhere else, and posted signs override all three.

cards.front: When may you exceed the limit by ten miles per hour?
cards.back: On two-lane highways posted at fifty-five miles per hour or higher you may go up to ten miles per hour over the limit, but only while lawfully passing another vehicle.

cards.front: How does driving faster affect crash risk?
cards.back: Driving faster shortens the time you have to react, raises the odds of a crash and makes serious injury or death in a crash more likely.

cards.front: What happens to your right-of-way if you reach an intersection at an unlawful speed?
cards.back: A driver who reaches an intersection at an unlawful speed gives up the right-of-way they would have had at a lawful speed.

decks.domain: Traffic laws: speed, signaling, lanes, turns, roundabouts, J-turns, U-turns and passing

cards.front: When do extra speeding fines apply?
cards.back: Speeding can bring a fine, and extra fines apply when you drive twenty miles per hour or more above the posted limit.

cards.front: What happens if you drive faster than one hundred miles per hour?
cards.back: Driving faster than one hundred miles per hour leads to revocation of your driving privileges for at least six months.

cards.front: What must you do when passing a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights?
cards.back: You must slow down when approaching or passing a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing emergency lights, and breaking this rule adds a surcharge of at least twenty-five dollars to the speeding fine.

cards.front: How do the penalties for twenty over and for over one hundred differ?
cards.back: Going twenty miles per hour or more over the limit adds extra fines, while going over one hundred miles per hour costs your driving privileges for at least six months.

cards.front: What does higher speed do to your field of vision?
cards.back: Higher speed narrows your field of vision as well as raising the risk of a crash.

cards.front: Which roadway hazards call for reducing speed?
cards.back: Watch for flag persons, pedestrians, barricades, flares or reflectors in the roadway and reduce speed for them, as well as in bad weather and on poor road surfaces.

cards.front: Which road shapes and features call for slower speeds?
cards.back: Reduce speed on narrow or winding roads and as you near a curve, the top of a hill or a railroad crossing.

cards.front: Why slow down on gravel or dirt roads?
cards.back: On gravel or dirt roads slow down, because stopping takes longer and the vehicle skids more easily in a turn.

cards.front: What special rules may apply on bridges?
cards.back: Bridges may carry their own speed limits and No Passing signs, and you must watch for and obey them.

decks.domain: Traffic laws: speed, signaling, lanes, turns, roundabouts, J-turns, U-turns and passing

cards.front: How far before a turn must you signal?
cards.back: Turn on your signal at least one hundred feet before you turn, and keep it on until the turn or lane change is finished.

cards.front: When may you use hand and arm signals?
cards.back: In daylight you may use hand and arm signals along with or in place of turn signals, but not at night or in a vehicle that hides your hand from other drivers.

cards.front: May you use hand signals at night?
cards.back: Hand and arm signals are a daylight option only; at night, or when your vehicle hides your arm, rely on the turn signals.

cards.front: Does a lane exist if it is not marked?
cards.back: A traffic lane exists whether or not it is marked, and you must stay inside one lane without weaving or straddling the markings.

cards.front: What should you do before changing lanes?
cards.back: Before changing lanes make sure there is room beside, behind and ahead of you, and turn your head to check the new lane instead of relying only on mirrors.

cards.front: What are blind spots and what creates them?
cards.back: Blind spots are areas your mirrors cannot show; the vehicle's design and roof pillars decide where they are, and a dirty windshield or glare can add temporary ones.

cards.front: Whose blind spots should you avoid driving in?
cards.back: Stay out of other drivers' blind spots, and pay special attention to them near commercial vehicles.

decks.domain: Traffic law confusables and continuation facts

cards.front: How do you avoid improper turns?
cards.back: Improper turns cause many crashes, so move into the correct lane well before the point where you will turn.

cards.front: What should you never do when turning?
cards.back: Never make a sudden turn from the wrong lane, watch for traffic or obstacles on the road you are entering, and always end the turn in the correct lane.

cards.front: How should your wheels point while you wait to turn?
cards.back: While you wait to turn, keep the wheels pointed straight and your foot on the brake so a rear-end hit is less likely to shove you into oncoming traffic.

cards.front: Where do you wait when turning left on green with oncoming traffic?
cards.back: When waiting to turn left on a green light with traffic coming toward you, pull into the intersection until your body lines up with the curb line, and you may only get to turn once the light turns yellow.

cards.front: What should you do when the car ahead signals a left turn?
cards.back: If the car ahead is signaling a left turn, slow down and get ready to stop.

cards.front: How do you make a left turn and where do you finish?
cards.back: For a left turn, check behind you and signal, move into the lane nearest the center line, or just right of the road's center if lanes are unmarked, look both ways, yield if needed, and finish in the first lane to the right of the center line.
cards.memory_hook: Center lane in, right of center

cards.front: How do you make a right turn and where do you finish?
cards.back: For a right turn, check behind you and signal, move close to the right curb, look both ways, yield if needed, and finish in the lane next to the curb.

cards.front: Where do left and right turns finish, and how do you steer?
cards.back: A left turn ends in the first lane to the right of the center line, while a right turn ends in the lane next to the curb, and both use hand-over-hand steering.
cards.memory_hook: Left near center, right by curb

cards.front: How do you drive through multiple turn lanes?
cards.back: Where signs or lane markings show two or more turning lanes, stay in your own lane all the way through the turn.

cards.front: When may you turn right on a red light?
cards.back: Many intersections allow a right turn on red after a complete stop in the correct lane, unless a No Turn on Red sign is posted, and only after checking every direction for pedestrians and traffic.

cards.front: When is a left turn on red allowed?
cards.back: A left turn on red is allowed in certain cases only when turning from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a complete stop and once the intersection is clear.

cards.front: How do the rules for right on red and left on red differ?
cards.back: A right turn on red is allowed at many intersections, but a left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, and both need a complete stop first.

cards.front: What should you watch for when turning right on red?
cards.back: When you turn right on red, watch for oncoming drivers turning left in front of you, since their green arrow may come on before your light turns green.

cards.front: What must you do whenever you turn on a red light?
cards.back: Whenever you turn on a red light, yield to traffic and pedestrians, and where a No Turn on Red sign is posted, wait for the green light.

decks.domain: Traffic law confusables and continuation facts

cards.front: Why are roundabouts used instead of four-way stops?
cards.back: Roundabouts are built to move traffic better and to make intersections safer than ordinary four-way stops.

cards.front: What should you do as you approach a roundabout?
cards.back: As you approach a roundabout, slow down, pick your lane before entering if it has more than one lane, yield to pedestrians and bicyclists crossing, and watch for signs or markings that require or forbid certain moves.

cards.front: When may you enter a roundabout?
cards.back: Enter a roundabout only after yielding to vehicles already circulating and after all traffic coming from your left has cleared.

cards.front: How do you drive once inside a roundabout?
cards.back: Inside a roundabout drive counterclockwise to your exit and never stop, pass or change lanes.

cards.front: What do you do if an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout?
cards.back: If an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout, leave the roundabout right away and then pull over.

cards.front: Which vehicles may leave their lane in a roundabout?
cards.back: Any combination vehicle, or a vehicle over forty feet long or more than ten feet wide, may leave its lane as needed to get through a roundabout while watching other traffic.

cards.front: Who yields when two large vehicles go through a multi-lane roundabout together?
cards.back: Entering cars yield to cars already in the roundabout, but when two large vehicles go through a multi-lane roundabout side by side, the driver on the right yields to the one on the left, slowing or stopping if needed.

cards.front: Why are J-turns built on divided highways?
cards.back: J-turns exist to cut deaths and injuries from broadside crashes on four-lane divided highways.

cards.front: How do you cross or turn left using a J-turn?
cards.back: At a J-turn every side-street driver turns right; to cross or go left you stop completely, turn right onto the highway, move into the marked left-turn lane at the median opening and make a U-turn.

cards.front: May you cross both lanes in one motion at a J-turn?
cards.back: During the right turn at a J-turn you may cross both lanes into the left-turn lane in a single motion when it is safe, which shortens your time in the through lanes.
cards.memory_hook: Both lanes at once if safe

cards.front: What must you do when finishing the U-turn at a J-turn?
cards.back: When finishing the U-turn at a J-turn you must yield to oncoming traffic, stopping if needed, before entering the through lanes.

cards.front: How may you cross a rural divided highway with a wide median?
cards.back: When a rural divided highway has enough room between its roadways, you may cross one half, wait in the middle to the right of center, and cross the second half when it is safe.

cards.front: What extra care does turning left onto a divided highway need?
cards.back: Turning left onto a divided highway follows the same steps as crossing it, and you must leave enough room that you do not slow oncoming traffic while you speed up.

decks.domain: Traffic law confusables and continuation facts

cards.front: When is a U-turn allowed?
cards.back: A U-turn reverses your direction with a half-circle turn, is allowed only when it will not disrupt other traffic, and is forbidden wherever a No U-Turn sign is posted.

cards.front: Where are U-turns banned?
cards.back: U-turns are banned on interstate freeways, and also near hilltops or on curves where drivers coming toward you could not see you from one thousand feet away.
cards.memory_hook: No U-turns on freeways or blind

cards.front: How may you make a U-turn on a road with two or more lanes your way?
cards.back: On a roadway with two or more lanes in your direction, you may swing into the farthest lane and briefly use the shoulder to finish a U-turn when needed.

cards.front: Where must a slow driver stay on a road with one lane each way?
cards.back: With only one lane in your direction, a driver going slowly enough to create a hazard must stay as close as possible to the right curb or road edge.

cards.front: Which lane should you use on a highway with several lanes your way?
cards.back: On highways with more than one lane in your direction, use the right-hand lane when one is available, and leave the left-most lane to let another vehicle pass when practical.

cards.front: When may you use a lane other than the right-hand lane?
cards.back: You may use a lane other than the right-hand lane when passing, preparing a left turn at an intersection or into a driveway, preparing a left-side exit from an expressway, freeway or interstate, driving an authorized emergency vehicle, or following a traffic control device, a peace officer or work zone directions.

decks.domain: Traffic law confusables and continuation facts

cards.front: What should you check before passing?
cards.back: Take extra care passing at night, in poor visibility or on slippery roads, and before passing make sure oncoming traffic is far enough away and that nobody behind you is starting to pass.

cards.front: How do you signal and return when passing?
cards.back: Signal left before moving out to pass and signal right after passing, then return to the right lane once the whole vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror.

cards.front: How soon must you be back in your lane after passing?
cards.back: After passing you must be back on the right side of the road before you come within one hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle.

cards.front: Which two passing rules both use one hundred feet?
cards.back: On the passing page one hundred feet appears twice: you must be back in the right lane before you are within one hundred feet of an oncoming vehicle, and you may not pass within one hundred feet of an intersection, underpass, tunnel or railroad crossing.

cards.front: Where may you not pass?
cards.back: You may not pass where a No Passing Zone sign is posted or where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line, and double solid yellow lines forbid passing in both directions.

cards.front: How do single and double solid yellow lines differ for passing?
cards.back: A single solid yellow line on your side bans passing for you, while a double solid yellow line bans passing for drivers in both directions.

cards.front: How much clear road must you see ahead to pass on a hill or curve?
cards.back: Never pass on a hill or curve unless you can clearly see at least seven hundred feet of road ahead.

cards.front: Near which places is passing not allowed?
cards.back: Passing is not allowed within one hundred feet of an intersection, an underpass, a tunnel or a railroad crossing.

cards.front: What should you do when another driver is passing you?
cards.back: Do not pass when you are about to meet an oncoming vehicle, and when someone is passing you, stay in your lane and do not speed up.

cards.front: When may you pass on the right?
cards.back: You may pass on the right only when it is safe and the vehicle ahead is turning or about to turn left, or the road has room for two or more lanes of moving traffic each way, or it is a one-way road wide enough for two or more lanes with nothing in the way.

cards.front: May you use the shoulder or a bike lane to pass on the right?
cards.back: A pass on the right must stay on the main roadway: using a bike lane, the shoulder or the unpaved edge to get around a vehicle is not allowed.

cards.front: May you back up on a freeway or expressway?
cards.back: Backing up on freeways or expressways is not allowed except for emergency vehicles on duty, and backing on public roads can lead to a reckless or careless driving charge.

cards.front: How should you back out of a driveway?
cards.back: Leaving a driveway in reverse, back only into the closest lane and then pull forward, and never reverse into or across traffic lanes unless you are sure it is safe.

recap_hooks.text: Keep right on wide roads except for the listed reasons, and drive at a speed reasonable for conditions, never above the posted limit.
Without signs the limits are ten in alleys, thirty on urban or town roads and fifty-five elsewhere, with ten over allowed only while passing on fast two-lane highways.
Twenty or more over brings extra fines, over one hundred brings at least six months' revocation, and skipping the emergency vehicle slow-down adds a surcharge.
Slow down for roadway hazards, curves, hills, crossings, gravel roads and bad weather.
Signal at least one hundred feet before turning, and use hand signals only in daylight.
Stay inside one lane and turn your head to check blind spots before changing lanes.
Get into the correct lane early, wait with wheels straight, and finish left turns right of center and right turns by the curb.
Right on red is allowed at many intersections after a full stop, but left on red only from a one-way onto a one-way street.
In a roundabout, yield to traffic already circling, travel counterclockwise and never stop, pass or change lanes.
At a J-turn, turn right, move into the left-turn lane, make a U-turn and yield before entering the through lanes.
U-turns are banned on interstate freeways and where oncoming drivers could not see you from one thousand feet.
Use the right lane when available, except when passing, turning left, exiting left, driving an emergency vehicle or following directions.
See seven hundred feet ahead before passing on hills or curves, and be back in your lane before one hundred feet from oncoming traffic.
Solid yellow on your side bans your pass, double yellow bans everyone, and no passing within one hundred feet of crossings and intersections.
